content: Cyclospora cayetanensis is a protozoan organism that causes disease in humans and potentially in other primates. It has also been isolated from the feces of animals such as ducks and chickens. The spherical shape of its sporocysts led to its classification within the Cyclospora genus. This organism possesses a double-layered wall, which provides resistance to disinfectants, and adhesins that contribute to its ability to adhere to surfaces. Cyclospora cayetanensis exhibits a tropism for the epithelial cells of the small intestine, particularly the duodenum and jejunum. Taxonomically, Cyclospora cayetanensis belongs to the Eukaryota domain, Alveolata superphylum, Apicomplexa phylum, Conoidasida class, Coccidia subclass, Eucoccidiorida order, Eimeriorina suborder, Eimeriidae family, and Cyclospora genus. Biologically, Cyclospora cayetanensis is an obligate intracellular apicomplexan protozoan that forms cysts and belongs to the Eimeriidae family. It is a common cause of self-limiting diarrhea. Morphologically, it measures between 5 and 10 micrometers in diameter and has a bilayered wall approximately 50 nanometers thick, with an outer threadlike coat described as wrinkled by some researchers. Phylogenetic analysis of the 18S rRNA gene has shown that Cyclospora species isolated from baboons are similar to Cyclospora cayetanensis that infects humans, placing them in the same clade as Eimeria species. Additional Cyclospora species, such as C. cercopitheci, C. colobi, and C. papionis, have been identified in green monkeys, colobus monkeys, and baboons, respectively. These species, including C. cayetanensis, are host-specific. Light microscopy cannot differentiate between these morphologically similar species. The exact environmental conditions and locations required for oocyst sporulation remain unknown, but understanding these factors could help predict the distribution and seasonality of Cyclospora cayetanensis. Its double-layered wall makes it highly resistant to disinfectants, particularly those used in food processing. This resistance, combined with its strong binding affinity to certain produce, explains the risks associated with contaminated foods. The adhesive properties of Cyclospora cayetanensis are stronger than those of Giardia or Cryptosporidium oocysts, although the specific adhesins responsible have not yet been identified. Cyclospora cayetanensis demonstrates a specific tropism for the epithelial cells of the small intestine, with a particular preference for the jejunum. The natural reservoir of Cyclospora cayetanensis is humans, as it is a host-specific parasite. Cyclospora oocysts have also been isolated from the feces of various animals, including ducks, chickens, and dogs. However, attempts to infect other animals with Cyclospora cayetanensis have been unsuccessful. Certain shellfish may acquire Cyclospora cayetanensis from contaminated waters and concentrate its oocysts for several days. In terms of differential diagnosis, Cyclospora cayetanensis infection must be distinguished from other causes of viral, bacterial, and parasitic gastroenteritis. Small bowel diarrhea caused by Cyclospora cayetanensis is typically watery and voluminous, with fewer than 5 white blood cells (WBCs) per high-power field. In contrast, large bowel diarrhea is characterized by mucous or bloody stools, lower volume, and more than 10 WBCs per high-power field. The severity of infection can vary, with oocyst counts reaching as high as 1,000 depending on the patient’s immune status.
